title: C++ Rule of 3, 5 & 0 — When to Define Copy, Move & Destructor
description:
A complete walkthrough of one of C++'s most important class-design principles — when to define the special member functions and when to let the compiler handle them. We cover all three rules with examples and the compiler-generation rules that catch most developers off guard:

- The 5 special member functions: destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment, move constructor, move assignment
- Rule of Three — if you define any of {destructor, copy ctor, copy assignment}, you usually need all three
- Why it matters: shallow copy, double-delete, dangling pointers, memory leaks
- Rule of Five (C++11) — same idea, extended to move semantics
- Live example: deep copy for a class holding a raw pointer
- Rule of Zero — if you don't manage a resource directly, define none of them
- Compiler-generation rules every interviewer asks about:
    - Define a destructor → move ctor & move assignment are implicitly deleted
    - Define a move ctor → copy operations are implicitly deleted
    - Classes with const, reference, or unique_ptr members → compiler can't auto-generate copy
- When to use which rule in real-world class design


Essential for C++ interview prep and writing safe, modern C++ code.
